Пайк выписали из местной больницы, и сейчас она находится в исправительно-реабилитационном центре имени Дебры К. Джонсон, где её содержали более 30 лет.
В среду адвокаты сообщили, что 50-летняя Пайк, приговоренная к смертной казни за убийство, совершенное в 1995 году, на этой неделе пришла в себя в больнице «разъяренной и озадаченной». Впереди её ждёт длительное восстановление после того, как она пережила попытку казни 30 сентября.
Ранее её защитники предполагали, что у женщины могла наступить смерть мозга.
После того как две инъекции не смогли вызвать её смерть в тюрьме строгого режима Ривербенд, Пайк в бессознательном состоянии доставили из камеры для казней в больницу в Нэшвилле. Она находилась в критическом состоянии и имела тяжелые повреждения рук.
На этой неделе судья штата Теннесси обязал представителей властей сохранить все доказательства, связанные с неудачной попыткой её казни. Один из адвокатов Пайк назвал это решение «первым из многих шагов по сохранению и обеспечению её конституционных прав».
Губернатор Теннесси Билл Ли приостановил все казни до конца года, пока следователи расследуют обстоятельства неудачной казни Пайк и аналогичного инцидента с Тони Каррутерсом в мае, когда сотрудники тюрьмы не смогли установить внутривенные катетеры.

sources.news_title: Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike released from hospital, returned to prison
sources.text:
U.S. death row inmate Christa Pike was released from a US hospital on Saturday and sent back to prison, where she will continue receiving medical care following her botched execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said.
Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years, said attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the Tennessee Office of the Post Conviction Defender in a joint release.
Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in the hospital this week, with a long recuperation ahead after surviving the attempted execution on September 30, her lawyers said on Wednesday. They previously believed she could be brain-dead.
Pike, 50, had been taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
A Tennessee judge this week ordered State officials to preserve all evidence related to their failed attempt to execute her, a development one of her lawyers called the “first of many steps to preserve and enforce her constitutional rights.”
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched execution of Pike and a similar failure involving Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.

sources.text:
Tennessee death row inmate discharged from hospital after surviving botched execution
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has been sent back to the women’s prison she had spent three decades in, her lawyers have said
Death row inmate Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder in the US state of Tennessee, has been discharged from a local hospital after surviving a botched execution. The woman was sent back to prison on Saturday, days after regaining her ability to walk and talk after receiving a double lethal injection, her lawyers have said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Her execution, which was scheduled for September 30, was expected to be the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The inmate did not lose her consciousness after two syringes of pentobarbital were administered and complained about feeling pain in her arm instead. She eventually lost consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily and snoring as well as still had a heartbeat nearly 90 minutes into the execution, prompting an ambulance to take her to a hospital, according to the US media.
The woman initially remained unconscious and was on a ventilator. According to The Guardian, she was allegedly declared brain dead on Monday before suddenly regaining her consciousness on Thursday. One of her lawyers said at the time she was “up and walking,” even though she was “somewhat foggy.”
On Saturday, Pike was returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she had spent 30 years. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” her lawyers said, adding that the woman “is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.”
The authorities provided no official explanation as to why Pike survived the execution. The New York Times reported earlier, citing medical experts, that Pike probably survived the procedure because the lethal drug leaked into tissue around the insertion sites instead of entering her bloodstream. The woman’s lawyers had previously warned that her medical history, including a blood-clotting condition, and small veins increased the risk that she would experience unnecessary pain.
The incident prompted the resignation of Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. The state’s governor, Bill Lee, also ordered an independent review of the botched execution and suspended the only other execution scheduled for this year. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis cancelled a planned lethal injection execution in his state as well on Friday.
Pike, then aged 18, was convicted of first-degree murder after she, her boyfriend, and another accomplice lured Slemmer, a fellow student, to an isolated area near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus, where Pike brutally beat her and cut her throat.
Her case became the second botched execution in Tennessee this year. In May, the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers was halted after the officials repeatedly failed to establish intravenous access to administer pentobarbital. The governor then granted the man a one-year reprieve as he was returned to death row. The incident raised questions about the state’s lethal injection procedures months before Pike’s execution.

Despite showing some signs of recovery, she continues to stay under medical observation. In fact, her case has also raised serious questions about Tennessee's lethal injection procedures.
Christa Pike returns to prison after a hospital stay
Christa Pike's attorneys have confirmed that she has been discharged from the hospital. In fact, she has also returned to the women's prison where she spent approximately 30 years of her life. According to the statement shared by her legal team, Christa was grateful to the first responders and medical professionals who treated her after the failed execution.
Her lawyers have mentioned that she will continue to get medical care in prison. Meanwhile, the doctors and medical staff are expected to monitor her condition as she recovers from the injuries and complications.
The 50-year-old's return to prison is a major development in Christa Pike's recovery after an execution, which went completely wrong. However, her discharge does not mean that she has fully recovered. Rather, the death row inmate has described that the experience was severely traumatic for her. Therefore, the effects of the incident will continue to impact Christa in the long run.
For those who don't know, Christa has made progress in her physical recovery. Her legal team also mentioned that doctors are impressed by her improvement. In fact, she has also started eating and regained her ability to walk with physical assistance. Despite these developments, Christa still has some serious injuries. Her arms were severely burned and blistered after receiving two doses of pentobarbital during the execution attempt. She was also treated for a blood clot in her arm and pneumonia during her hospital stay.
Initially, Christa's condition was more critical. She was reportedly placed on life support and declared brain dead before she unexpectedly gained consciousness and began to speak. Since then, she has shown signs of improvement, but her attorney says she remains mentally foggy and is struggling to understand what happened to her.
However, Christa's survival of the lethal injection has brought more scrutiny to the state's execution process. Her legal team has explained that the incident was deeply distressing and she sustained both the physical injuries and the psychological trauma that she has faced. A judge has ordered the Tennessee Department of Corrections to preserve the evidence linked to the failed execution. In turn, they will examine what went wrong inside the execution chamber and whether the procedures were properly followed or not.
According to the information provided, Tennessee has indicated that no further executions will happen until at least 2027. So, any future legal proceedings would focus on understanding the situation around Christa's treatment and execution.
What is Christa Pike's case about?
Christa Pike was sentenced to death in 1995 for the murder of a 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, Tennessee. At that time, she was 18 and attending a Job Corps training program with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and Colleen. Some prosecutors said that the killing was caused by jealousy. Eventually, on January 12, 1995, Christa, Tadaryl, and another young woman, Shadolla Peterson, called Slemmer to an isolated place near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus.
Christa and Tadaryl then attacked her, beating and stabbing her. In turn, Colleen suffered a major injury with a skull fracture. Christa was then found guilty of first-degree murder and conspiracy and sentenced to death in 1996. Meanwhile, Tadaryl got a life sentence with the possibility of parole, while Shadolla got a lesser sentence because she cooperated with the authorities. Later, Christa was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder in 2001 when she attacked a fellow inmate, which added 25 years to her sentence.

The US death row inmate who survived a failed lethal injection in Tennessee has been discharged from hospital and returned to prison, the Associated Press reports.
Christa Pike, 50, was transferred to the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, the women’s prison where she had been held for 30 years, her attorneys said in a statement on Saturday.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said.
Pike had been hospitalised since September 30, when Tennessee officials attempted to execute her by lethal injection for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.
She survived two doses of pentobarbital, the drug used in the execution. At one point, she was placed on a ventilator, and her attorneys feared she would not survive.
However, she later regained consciousness and began talking and walking with assistance.
The Death Penalty Information Centre said Pike was the first known person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
Tennessee officials have not explained what went wrong during the execution attempt. Medical and lethal injection experts have examined whether improperly placed intravenous lines prevented the drug from entering Pike’s bloodstream as intended.
In a court filing, Pike’s attorneys said “apparently, at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”
The failed execution has prompted renewed scrutiny of Tennessee’s execution procedures.
Governor Bill Lee postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of the incident, while the state’s prison chief resigned in its aftermath.

Her attorneys filed an emergency motion in Davidson County Chancery Court last week seeking an order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence related to the execution attempt.
A judge granted the motion during a hearing on Wednesday.
According to the motion, Pike "could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly" while being administered two lethal doses of pentobarbital, at one point stating that her arm "feels like it's about to burst open."
At least seven needles were used to gain IV access, with one "bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the motion stated.

She was initially on a ventilator following the execution attempt before regaining consciousness on Tuesday, her attorneys said.

sources.text:
Christa Pike has been released from the hospital and returned to prison after surviving a botched execution attempt, according to a statement from her legal team.
"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of
Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the TN Office of the Post Conviction Defender, said in a statement emailed to Newsweek Saturday.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the statement continued. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after Tennessee attempted to execute her by lethal injection on September 30. She survived after receiving two doses of pentobarbital.
Her attorneys announced on October 6 that she had regained consciousness and was speaking. Two days later, they said she was walking with assistance, eating a regular diet and regaining movement and strength in her arms.
Pike was convicted of killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a Job Corps training program in Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time.
On January 12, 1995, Pike, her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson lured Slemmer into a wooded area, where she was attacked and killed. Pike and Shipp were later convicted in connection with the killing, while Peterson pleaded guilty and received probation.
Pike received a death sentence in 1996. Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the crime, received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike’s survival has brought renewed scrutiny to Tennessee's lethal-injection procedures and raised questions about whether the state could attempt to execute her again. Republican Governor Bill Lee has ordered a third-party review of what went wrong and paused the state's remaining execution scheduled for this year. Gary Wayne Sutton had been scheduled to be executed on December 3.
Tennessee prison chief Frank Strada stepped down last week following the failed execution.
Meanwhile, Pike's lawyers have said they will continue asking Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
Timeline of Christa Pike's Botched Execution and Recovery
September 30: Tennessee attempted to execute Pike at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. The U.S. Supreme Court lifted a stay shortly before 6 p.m., allowing the execution to proceed. After receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike remained alive and was taken to a hospital.
October 1: Pike's attorneys said she was alive, in critical condition and receiving “life-saving medical care.” They also began publicly raising concerns about the process used to establish IV access during the execution.
October 5: Her attorneys were told by medical professionals there was a possibility that she was brain-dead and might need to be removed from life support, according to a later account from her legal team.
October 6: Her attorneys announced that Pike was conscious and speaking. They described her recovery as “medically unprecedented,” while cautioning that her prognosis remained unclear.
October 7: Her legal team reported that Pike was confused and angry and still had significant bruising to her arms, pneumonia and a blood clot. Separate reporting said she had begun taking limited steps with assistance.
October 8: Her attorneys said Pike was walking “with some assistance,” that her arms were “healing and regaining movement and strength,” her lungs were clear and she had started eating a regular diet.
October 10: Pike was discharged from the hospital and returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where her attorneys said she would continue receiving medical care.
What Happened During Christa Pike's Botched Execution
The September 30 botched execution followed hours of legal uncertainty. After a stay delayed proceedings, the U.S. Supreme Court lifted it shortly before 6 p.m., clearing the way for Tennessee to proceed.
During the execution, Pike received two doses of pentobarbital but continued breathing. Witnesses reported hearing her breathing and snoring after the drug was administered and the blinds to the execution chamber were closed. She was eventually transported to the hospital.
Pike's attorneys have raised questions about the state's efforts to establish IV access. Spivey said execution staff used at least seven needles on her left arm and that one needle was bent when it was removed. He also said there was blistering and burning around injection sites.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has said it followed its execution protocol.
A Davidson County chancery judge has ordered the preservation of evidence connected to the execution attempt.
What Experts Say
Medical and legal experts say Christa Pike’s failed execution raises separate concerns about how lethal injections are carried out and whether Tennessee could constitutionally attempt to execute her again.
Jonathan Groner, a former surgeon and expert on the medical aspects of capital punishment, recently told Newsweek that lethal injection presents what he called a “Hippocratic paradox” because medical professionals best qualified to administer drugs are constrained by professional ethics from participating in executions.
“The problem with lethal injection is the people who are most qualified to do it are ethically forbidden from participating,” Groner said. “It’s also the only medical procedure where incompetence saves lives.”
He said problems with intravenous access could help explain how Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital, raising the possibility that the drug did not enter her bloodstream as intended.
Separately, Deborah Denno, a Fordham University School of Law professor who specializes in the death penalty, previously told Newsweek that Pike’s attorneys could argue that another execution attempt would violate the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy because Tennessee carried out the procedure it intended to perform.
“The state has one bite of the apple,” Denno said. “They can't come back and say, ‘Well, we didn't do it right.’”
Denno distinguished Pike’s case from the 1947 Supreme Court case Louisiana ex rel. Francis v. Resweber, which allowed Louisiana to try again after an electric chair malfunctioned during Willie Francis’ first execution attempt. In Pike’s case, she said, Tennessee successfully established IV access and administered the execution drug twice.
“They found IV access. They injected the drugs. They did it twice,” Denno said. “They actually went through the execution process twice.”
Denno stressed that the double-jeopardy argument has not been decided by a court and could face significant legal hurdles. She said Pike could also raise an Eighth Amendment challenge if Tennessee seeks another lethal injection, particularly given the pain and injuries alleged during the first attempt.
“I think there’s a very good argument that for her, lethal injection was a cruel and unusual punishment,” Denno said. “Certainly in her case, there would be a risk of severe pain because there already has been.”
Slemmer's Mother Reacts
May Martinez, Slemmer's mother, said after learning that Pike was awake and speaking that she had believed Pike would survive and did not expect Tennessee to try again.
Asked what she wanted to happen next, Martinez told local news station WBIR: “It doesn’t matter what I think, they’re going to do what they’re going to do.”
Martinez traveled to Nashville to witness the September 30 execution and was present when it failed.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” she told the Associated Press on October 1.

Según el comunicado, Pike agradece a los servicios de emergencia y a su equipo médico la atención recibida “en estas circunstancias extraordinarias”. Sus abogados indicaron que seguirá recibiendo cuidados médicos dentro de la prisión y que continuarán monitoreando su recuperación.
Cómo evoluciona su salud
El País, citando a los abogados, reportó que el miércoles Pike comenzó a dar “pequeños pasos” con ayuda y que el jueves caminaba con cierta asistencia. Sus brazos, donde se inyectaron las dosis, se estaban recuperando, había empezado a alimentarse con normalidad y tenía los pulmones limpios.
Días antes, el martes 6 de octubre, sus abogados habían informado de que estaba despierta y hablando, seis días después del intento de ejecución que la dejó inconsciente y con respirador.
Qué ocurrió el 30 de septiembre
Según sus abogados, Pike recibió dos dosis de pentobarbital sin que se produjera su muerte.
El Departamento de Corrección de Tennessee (TDOC) emitió esa noche un aviso a medios en el que afirmó haber seguido cada paso del protocolo de ejecución aprobado por la Fiscalía General, y que el protocolo no permite procedimientos adicionales a los realizados. El mismo aviso informó del traslado de Pike a un centro médico externo.
La agencia AP señaló que el TDOC no ha explicado qué salió mal. Según el medio, el departamento declinó comentar por qué falló el intento y si planea volver a intentar ejecutarla.
El Centro de Información sobre la Pena de Muerte (DPIC) sostiene que Pike es la primera persona que sobrevive tras recibir los fármacos de inyección letal durante una ejecución.
Lo que alega la defensa
Los abogados de Pike sostienen que el intento fallido constituye un castigo “cruel e inusual”. Según El País, también afirman que desde enero habían cuestionado el protocolo porque las venas de la reclusa eran de difícil acceso. Aseguran que se usaron al menos siete agujas, una de ellas doblada en un ángulo de 90 grados, y que el personal no detectó que el pentobarbital se filtraba fuera de la vena. Estas son afirmaciones de la defensa; el TDOC no se ha pronunciado sobre ellas.
Pese a la oposición de la fiscalía, la jueza I’Ashea Myles ordenó conservar los materiales, la documentación y los residuos del intento de ejecución, como pidió la defensa. Según los fiscales, corresponde al Tribunal Supremo de Tennessee decidir si se repite la ejecución.
El gobernador Bill Lee ordenó una revisión integral por un tercero para determinar exactamente lo ocurrido y descartó la ejecución que quedaba programada este año.
Los abogados de Pike han pedido al gobernador conmutar su pena por cadena perpetua sin libertad condicional.
